What SolidWorks Actually Needs From Hardware

Before looking at prices, it helps to know where SolidWorks spends its time. Most everyday modelling work, such as rebuilding features, editing sketches and updating part history, runs largely on one CPU core. That is why a processor with high clock speeds often feels faster in SolidWorks than a chip with more cores and lower clocks.

Other tasks scale differently:

  • Rendering (Visualize, PhotoView 360) uses many cores or the GPU, so core count and graphics power both matter.
  • Simulation benefits from more cores and more memory, especially with fine meshes.
  • Large assemblies lean on RAM capacity and fast NVMe storage for open and save times.
  • Viewport performance depends on the graphics card and its driver.

Entry CAD build: students and small parts

The Core Ultra 5 250K Plus offers strong single-thread speed for its price, which is what makes part modelling feel responsive. 32GB of DDR5 is the sensible starting point for SolidWorks today; 16GB fills up quickly once you open a few drawings alongside a browser and email. This tier suits students, freelancers and engineers working mainly on individual parts and small assemblies.

Professional build: daily engineering work

The Ryzen 9 9900X adds 12 cores with high boost clocks, so it handles both everyday modelling and occasional rendering without slowing down. The RTX 5070 drives large viewports and multiple monitors easily, and a Gen5 NVMe drive cuts open and save times on big files. This is the build we recommend to most engineering offices.

Heavy assemblies and simulation

The Ryzen 9 9950X brings 16 cores for simulation and rendering, while the ProArt X870E-Creator adds the connectivity and expansion that professional setups need. Pair it with 64GB of memory or more; large assemblies and fine simulation meshes use RAM quickly, and running out forces the system to page to disk.

Professional GPU or GeForce?

Dassault Systèmes certifies specific professional graphics cards and drivers for SolidWorks, such as NVIDIA’s RTX workstation range. Certified cards guarantee that every feature, including some advanced display modes, is supported and tested.

In practice, many engineers run SolidWorks well on GeForce cards, especially for modelling and rendering. The trade-off is support: if your company requires certified hardware, or you rely on features that only work on certified drivers, choose a professional card. We stock options such as the PNY NVIDIA RTX A4000 when available. Browse our graphics cards or ask us which route fits your licence and workflow.

Memory, Storage and Displays

Memory: 32GB is the minimum we recommend for SolidWorks in 2026, 64GB for large assemblies and simulation. Our RAM range covers DDR5 kits for both AMD and Intel platforms.

Storage: keep SolidWorks, your active projects and the local cache on a fast NVMe drive. A second drive or network storage for archives keeps the main drive from filling up. See our storage options for Gen4 and Gen5 drives.

Displays: two monitors, or one large high-resolution screen, make a real difference for CAD. Keep the model on one display and the feature tree, drawings or documentation on the other. A colour-accurate 27-inch panel at 1440p or 4K is a good fit; see our monitors.

Running a Workstation in Bahrain

CAD workstations often run long renders and simulations, and Bahrain’s heat adds stress during those sessions. We build workstations with generous airflow, good-quality power supplies and coolers sized for sustained loads rather than short gaming bursts. A UPS is worth adding for any machine doing long simulations, so a brief power cut does not cost you hours of work.

Buying locally also means warranty support in Bahrain. If a part fails, you deal with us directly instead of shipping components abroad, which matters when a workstation is how you earn a living.

How to Choose the Right Tier

Start with your largest typical file, not your average one. If your biggest assemblies open in under a minute on your current machine and you rarely render, the entry build will feel like a large upgrade. If you wait on rebuilds every day, render client visuals or share the machine between CAD and other heavy software, the professional tier pays for itself in saved hours.

Choose the heavy tier when simulation is part of your weekly work, or when assemblies run into thousands of components. In that case, put memory and the processor first and keep the graphics card sensible. Upgrading a GPU later is simple; changing platform is not.

Frequently Asked Questions

The case, cooler, Windows licence and assembly are extra. Contact us for an exact quote for your workload.

Is Intel or AMD better for SolidWorks?

Both work well. SolidWorks modelling depends mostly on single-core speed, which both current Intel Core Ultra and AMD Ryzen 9000 processors deliver. Choose AMD Ryzen 9 if you also render or run simulations, since the extra cores help there. For pure modelling on a budget, a Core Ultra 5 is a strong value.

How much RAM do I need for SolidWorks?

Start with 32GB of DDR5 for parts and small to medium assemblies. Move to 64GB if you work with large assemblies, run simulations with fine meshes, or keep several heavy applications open at once. Running out of memory slows SolidWorks far more than a slightly slower processor does.

Can I use an RTX 5070 for SolidWorks?

Yes, many users run SolidWorks on GeForce cards like the RTX 5070 for modelling and rendering. It is not on the certified hardware list, so some advanced display features may not be supported and official support can be limited. If your company requires certified hardware, choose an NVIDIA RTX professional card instead.

Is a gaming PC good enough for SolidWorks?

A well-balanced gaming PC often runs SolidWorks well, because both reward fast CPUs and good graphics. The differences are memory capacity, certified graphics drivers and cooling for long workloads. A workstation build prioritises those, which matters for daily professional use.
